messages.subject: Newbie question
parts:
My apologies if the answer is already here. I've tried to look and
probably missed it.

I have a CSV data file that contains first column with date time
information in a format that is POSIXct compatible. additional
columns(over 100 columns) contain numerical information(duh I know).
A heading line is in the file with column names. possibly 100000 rows
or more. Info is performance counters pulled from an Oracle database.

I can read in the file in to a dataframe in R with read.table.
I can attach the dataframe.

I can product single variable dot plots or line plots.

How do I produce a stacked area plot of all the columns at once? I've
looked at the ggplot2 docs and still don't get it.

I know it will be a mess, but this is the first step. Boiling it down
into something useful is the next step. Thought I'd try drawing the
picture first.

Please feel free to point me in the proper direction. Excel just isn't
big enough anymore.

Thanks in advance for you patience.

John

parts:
I wouldn't say newbie. I had a hard time with this one.

#make up some distribution data
df<-as.data.frame(cbind(0:20, dbinom(0:20,30, 0.15), dbinom(0:20,30,
0.5), dbinom(0:20, 30, 0.30)))
colnames(df)<- c("time", "col1", "col2", "col3")

#make up some dates 20 hours in 1 hour increments
library(chron)
t1 <- chron("1/1/2010", "00:00:00")
t2 <- chron("1/1/2010", "20:00:00")
tt <- seq(t1, t2, by = times("01:00:00"))
df[1]<-tt

#rearrange the dataframe in long format
melted.df<-melt(df, id.vars="time")

#areaplot
ggplot(melted.df, aes(x=time, y=value)) + geom_area(aes(fill=variable))

Does that help at all?

Seems to me that you need to take your very long data and make it even
longer with melt()/reshape().

I thought maybe you could use geom_bar() but it threw fits every time
I tried to do anything with it (see below).

Ok, I saw multiple references to melt. However, it just doesn't seem
to make sense to take a carefully crafted table of data and then cram
it all into one long 2 column array. That just seems marvelously
inefficient. It almost makes sense for small data sets but when one
single x variable is 100000+ samples, stringing lots of them together
one after another stops making sense fast. It also make performance
cost in generating such a graph horrendous. There has to be a better
answer.

I obviously need to do some boiling down of the data before pumping it
into ggplot. I guess I'll head back that way. I'll still need to plot
multiple high sample count variables in the end so the necessity for
an efficient method for generating plots still exists.

Just to give you an idea of the end game here, I have performance
statistics for an Oracle Database collected over a time span. I want
to statistically analyze them. Throw out the unimportant ones per that
analysis. Then, graph the remaining collections. The information
collected is basically microseconds spent doing various tasks within
the database engine. I can slice the data a number of ways and I do
that prior to feeding it thru R and ggplot.

Thanks,
john

messages.author: 9e1d805a26f6d719
messages.subject: Re: Newbie question
parts:
It's not just ggplot2. Most things in R assume that you have one row
per observation (which could include multiple dependent variables,
yielding multiple columns, in some cases, but I think not this one).
In your case, the various tasks (columns) are separate observations
with things in common. Think about doing a regression with that data.
The predictors would be indicators that indicate which column the data
point should be in. Converting to long format is just making the data
look like it should look to do a regression. And it's not any less
space efficient. So yes, long format it is if you want to use ggplot
with conditional plotting based on column (in your wide-format data
set).

This said, if you really have hundreds of thousands of data points in
various conditions, you weren't seriously thinking of plotting
millions of points on a single graph, were you? Even in ggplot, you'd
be plotting some sort of summary statistic. For smaller data sets,
ggplot can do a pretty good job of computing the summary statistics.
But in your case, you may want to compute the summaries (binning,
whatever) beforehand, then plot the results with ggplot directly.
Incidentally, the plyr package that ggplot2 relies on has recently
gotten substantially faster, as has the reshape package, which is now
called reshape2.

I think it'll make sense once you've done it, but yeah, it doesn't
make sense at first, especially if you're new to R's philosophical
quirks!

-Harlan

messages.subject: Re: Newbie question
parts:
Thanks to everyone that sent me suggestions. I managed to convince
ggplot to produce the output I was looking for. I did have to change
for format of the data I was providing.

At first it looked like

timestamp,1:event1,1:event2,2:event3,2:event4
13:24:22.765,32,0,0,754
13:24:22.883,0,15,8,623
13:24:23.547,41,0,11,0
13:24:24.353,0,0,7,98
...

Now it looks like
timestamp,inst_id,event,waiting
13:24:22.765,1,event1,32
13:24:22.765,1,event4,754
13:24:22.883,1,event2,15
13:24:22.883,2,event3,8
13:24:22.883,2,event4,623
...

# the following works to produce a giant stacked area plot!!
library(ggplot2)
datum<-read.table("event.txt",
header = TRUE,flush=TRUE,sep=",",stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
attach(datum)
ggplot(datum,aes(x=as.POSIXct(timestamp,tz="","%m-%d-%Y %H:%M:
%OS"),y=waiting))+
+ geom_area(aes(fill=event))

if I could make a fill of concatenated inst_id plus event that would
be great but this is good for now.

now to work on analyzing the data and filtering out what doesn't
actually matter.

Thanks,
John

2010/9/22 orclwzrd <orcl...@gmail.com>

Thanks to everyone that sent me suggestions. I managed to convince
ggplot to produce the output I was looking for. I did have to change
for format of the data I was providing.

At first it looked like

timestamp,1:event1,1:event2,2:event3,2:event4
13:24:22.765,32,0,0,754
13:24:22.883,0,15,8,623
13:24:23.547,41,0,11,0
13:24:24.353,0,0,7,98
...

Now it looks like
timestamp,inst_id,event,waiting
13:24:22.765,1,event1,32
13:24:22.765,1,event4,754
13:24:22.883,1,event2,15
13:24:22.883,2,event3,8
13:24:22.883,2,event4,623
...

# the following works to produce a giant stacked area plot!!
library(ggplot2)
datum<-read.table("event.txt",
          header = TRUE,flush=TRUE,sep=",",stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
attach(datum)
ggplot(datum,aes(x=as.POSIXct(timestamp,tz="","%m-%d-%Y %H:%M:
%OS"),y=waiting))+
+ geom_area(aes(fill=event))

if I could make a fill of concatenated inst_id plus event that would
be great but this is good for now.

now to work on analyzing the data and filtering out what doesn't
actually matter.

Thanks,
John
